metadata.title: The New Frontier in Research Ethics

params.text:
Welcome to the BriGRETE AI-enabled Research Ethics Training Module

Artificial Intelligence is rapidly transforming research across all scientific disciplines — from healthcare and social sciences to security and engineering. While these computational tools offer remarkable analytical capabilities, they simultaneously introduce complex ethical challenges that traditional research ethics frameworks may not fully address.

This module has been developed by the Institute of Informatics and Telecommunications, National Centre for Scientific Research “Demokritos” (authored by Dimitris Kyriazanos, with contributions by Xenia Douka and Vicky Mollaki), co-funded by the European Union under the BriGRETE Erasmus+ project.

Two Sub-Modules

  • Sub-Module 1 (Optional): Introduction to AI — key concepts and trending definitions for foundational understanding. This is the module you are currently taking.
  • Sub-Module 2: AI-enabled Research Ethics — the primary framework for evaluating AI components in research proposals.

params.alt: Who is this Training For? Three profiles: REC Members (evaluators of ethical aspects in research), Early Career Researchers (postgraduate students, PhD candidates, postdoctoral researchers), and Mid-Career & Senior Researchers (established researchers in domains disrupted by AI).

params.text:
Who is this Training For?

This module serves three distinct audience profiles:

  • REC Members: Evaluators of ethical aspects in research projects. This training assumes zero prior technical AI expertise, but focuses on data-driven methods and algorithmic decision-making.
  • Early Career Researchers: Postgraduate students, PhD candidates, and postdoctoral researchers who need foundational knowledge in AI ethics from the ground up.
  • Mid-Career & Senior Researchers: Established researchers in domains disrupted by AI (data management, interdisciplinary research) who need to selectively update their knowledge for advanced ethical engagement.

params.alt: Bridging the Gap: The training module acts as a bridge between Emerging AI Technologies on one side and Established Ethical Review Practices on the other. Four pillars: Support understanding of AI's ethical implications; Enhance the ability to review proposals involving AI; Promote a structured methodology aligned with legal frameworks; Drive thoughtful, informed, and proportionate evaluations.

params.text:
Purpose of the Module

The module acts as a functional bridge between two distinct worlds: the accelerating influx of emerging AI technologies, and the established ethical review practices that must govern their deployment in research.

Specifically, it aims to:

  • Support understanding of AI’s ethical implications in research.
  • Enhance the ability to review proposals involving AI components.
  • Promote a structured methodology aligned with existing legal and regulatory frameworks.
  • Drive thoughtful, informed, and proportionate evaluations.

params.alt: Core Competencies (Learning Objectives): Five steps — Recognize common types of AI used in research and their potential ethical impacts; Identify key ethical risks (bias, transparency, data protection, accountability); Apply core ethical principles to the evaluation of AI-driven research proposals; Ask relevant questions and request appropriate safeguards in proposals involving AI; Engage confidently with researchers on ethical issues specific to AI technologies.

params.text:
Learning Objectives

By the end of this training module, you will be able to:

  1. Recognize common types of AI used in research and their potential ethical impacts.
  2. Identify key ethical risks, including bias, lack of transparency, data protection issues, and accountability gaps.
  3. Apply core ethical principles to evaluate AI-driven research proposals.
  4. Ask relevant questions and request appropriate safeguards in proposals involving AI.
  5. Engage confidently with researchers on ethical issues specific to AI technologies.

Estimated duration: 30–40 minutes. No prior technical AI expertise required.

params.text:
What is Artificial Intelligence?

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the field of computer science focused on building systems capable of performing tasks that normally require human intelligence — including perception, reasoning, learning, and decision-making.

A Brief History

Understanding AI’s historical trajectory helps explain both its current power and its limitations:

  • 1950s: Alan Turing proposes the “Turing Test” as a measure of machine intelligence. John McCarthy coins the term “Artificial Intelligence” in 1956.
  • 1970s–80s: Early expert systems generate excitement, but unmet expectations lead to reduced funding and “AI winters.”
  • 1990s–2000s: Machine learning and statistical methods gain critical traction, quietly powering real-world applications.
  • 2010s–present: Deep learning, big data, and massive increases in computing power fuel the rapid AI progress we observe today.

The field took decades to reach today’s capabilities — it was not a sudden leap, but an incremental accumulation of data, hardware, and algorithmic insight.

params.title: Review key definitions and milestones from the history of AI.

dialogs.answer: The field of computer science focused on building systems capable of performing tasks that normally require human intelligence (perception, reasoning, learning, decision-making).

dialogs.answer: Alan Turing proposed it in the 1950s as a way to evaluate whether a machine could exhibit intelligent behaviour indistinguishable from a human.

dialogs.text: Who coined the term 'Artificial Intelligence' and when?
dialogs.answer: John McCarthy coined it in 1956 at the Dartmouth Conference.
Periods of reduced funding and interest in AI (primarily in the 1970s–80s) caused by unmet expectations from early expert systems.

dialogs.text: What three forces have driven AI progress since the 2010s?
dialogs.answer: Deep learning, big data (very large datasets), and massive increases in computational power.

params.text:
The AI Taxonomy: Three Nested Concepts

The terms AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning are frequently conflated in public discourse. Understanding their precise relationship is essential for accurate ethical analysis:

  • Artificial Intelligence (AI): The broadest category — a field aiming to simulate human intelligence in machines.
  • Machine Learning (ML): A subfield of AI where systems learn from data instead of being explicitly programmed with rules.
  • Deep Learning (DL): A subset of ML that uses multi-layered (“deep”) neural networks to model complex patterns in very large datasets.

Think of them as nested: every Deep Learning system is a Machine Learning system, and every Machine Learning system is an AI system — but not vice versa.

Robotics is an engineering discipline that overlaps with AI, but robots do not inherently require AI to function. A robotic arm on an assembly line may operate via fixed mechanical programming with no machine learning whatsoever.

panels.title: Misconception 2: 'AI' is always the correct label

params.text: The term 'AI' is frequently used as a marketing label for what are technically ML or DL applications. When reviewing a research proposal, look past the headline label and identify the specific algorithmic methodology in use.

panels.title: Why this matters for ethical review

params.text: The ethical risks of a rule-based expert system are fundamentally different from those of a deep learning model trained on human data. Accurate classification of the technology is the prerequisite for proportionate evaluation.

params.title: Test your understanding of the AI taxonomy.

dialogs.answer: A subfield of AI where systems learn from data instead of being explicitly programmed. The model improves its performance on a task through experience.
A subset of ML that uses deep (multi-layered) neural networks to model complex patterns in large datasets. Underlies most modern AI breakthroughs.

dialogs.text: How do AI, ML, and DL relate to each other?
dialogs.answer: They are nested: DL ⊂ ML ⊂ AI. All deep learning is machine learning, and all machine learning is AI — but not all AI is machine learning.
No. Robotics and AI are overlapping fields, but a robot may operate via fixed mechanical or rule-based programming without any AI or machine learning component.

dialogs.text: Why is 'AI' frequently used for ML/DL applications?
dialogs.answer: Primarily for marketing reasons. 'Artificial Intelligence' is a more commercially attractive label than the technically accurate 'machine learning model'.

params.text:
What Are Neural Networks?

Neural networks are computing systems loosely inspired by the architecture of the human brain. They consist of layers of interconnected artificial “neurons” that process vast amounts of input data, extract mathematical features, and learn patterns through iterative training.

Architecture

A standard neural network has three types of layers:

  • Input layer: Receives raw data (e.g., an image, a sentence, a tabular record).
  • Hidden layers: Intermediate layers where the network extracts increasingly abstract features through weighted connections between neurons.
  • Output layer: Produces the final prediction or classification.

“Deep” learning simply means the network has many hidden layers — enabling it to model highly complex relationships in data.

The 2012 Turning Point

Neural networks had existed theoretically for decades, but they only began to surpass traditional machine learning accuracy in 2012. This was not due to a sudden algorithmic breakthrough — it depended on two critical external factors: access to very large datasets, and a massive increase in computational hardware (particularly GPUs). Both conditions became available at scale in the early 2010s.

Ethical Implication

Because these networks function as dense, opaque calculation engines shaped entirely by ingested data, their primary ethical vulnerabilities are embedded in the data sourcing process — long before the model makes a single decision.

dialogs.text: What was the 2012 Turning Point for Neural Networks?

dialogs.text: What two resources do neural networks critically depend on?

dialogs.text: What is an advantage of deep neural networks over traditional machine learning?
dialogs.answer: Automatic feature extraction — neural networks learn relevant features from raw data without needing them to be manually defined by a human engineer.

params.text:
Natural Language Processing (NLP)

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is an interdisciplinary field at the intersection of computer science, artificial intelligence, and computational linguistics. Its core focus is enabling computers to understand, analyse, and generate human language.

NLP powers applications ranging from search engines and machine translation to chatbots and text summarisation tools.

Large Language Models (LLMs)

Large Language Models (LLMs) are a specific class of AI model trained on massive text datasets to simulate human-like language generation. They excel at summarisation, translation, and code generation.

The Illusion of Understanding

LLMs do not understand language in the human sense. Their core operating principle is deceptively simple: next-word prediction. Given a sequence of preceding words, the model calculates the statistical probability of each possible next word and selects accordingly. Chaining these predictions together produces fluent, coherent sentences — but the model has no comprehension of meaning, no beliefs, and no intent.

For example: given the phrase “The researcher analyzes the…”, an LLM assigns a high probability (e.g., 85%) to “data”, a lower probability to “sample”, and a small probability to “room”. The coherence of the output is a product of statistical frequency in training data, not reasoning.

Why this matters for research ethics

Anthropomorphising LLMs — attributing human intent, reasoning, or factual comprehension to their output — leads to severe methodological and ethical errors. An LLM that generates a plausible-sounding research summary is not “checking the facts”; it is predicting statistically likely word sequences.

params.title: Review NLP and LLM concepts.

dialogs.answer: An interdisciplinary field at the intersection of computer science, AI, and computational linguistics, focused on enabling computers to understand, analyse, and generate human language.
AI models trained on vast amounts of text data to understand and generate human-like language. They excel at summarisation, translation, and code generation.

dialogs.text: What is the core mechanical principle of LLMs?
dialogs.answer: Next-word prediction: the model calculates the statistical probability of each possible next word in a sequence and selects accordingly. It does not understand meaning.
The seemingly human-like output of LLMs, which is actually produced entirely through statistical pattern-matching on training data, not through genuine comprehension.

dialogs.text: Name three specific tasks at which LLMs excel.
dialogs.answer: Summarisation, translation, and code generation.

dialogs.text: Why is it problematic to anthropomorphise LLMs?
dialogs.answer: Because LLMs rely on statistical patterns, not reasoning or comprehension. Attributing human intent to their output invites methodological and ethical errors in research.

params.text:
What is Generative AI?

Generative AI refers to models capable of creating new, original content by extrapolating from patterns learned during training. Unlike traditional AI systems that classify or predict from existing data, generative models produce novel outputs.

Four Modalities of Generative AI

Generative AI operates across four primary content modalities:

  • Text Generation: Large Language Models (e.g., GPT-series) that produce written content, summaries, translations, and code.
  • Image Synthesis: Models (e.g., DALL·E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion) that generate realistic or artistic images from text prompts.
  • Audio Production: Models that generate speech, music, or sound effects from text or audio inputs.
  • Video Creation: Models (e.g., Sora by OpenAI) that generate video sequences from text or image prompts.

All generative outputs are extrapolations of statistical patterns in training data — not original human creativity. This distinction is important when evaluating research that uses generative AI to produce, augment, or analyse data.

params.title: Review Generative AI concepts.

dialogs.answer: AI models capable of creating new, original content (text, images, audio, or video) based on patterns learned from training data.

dialogs.text: Which AI model is associated with video generation?
dialogs.answer: Sora, developed by OpenAI, is a generative AI model for creating video content.

dialogs.text: Which AI model is associated with image synthesis?
dialogs.answer: DALL·E (by OpenAI) is a well-known example of a generative AI model for image synthesis.

dialogs.text: Name all four modalities of Generative AI.
dialogs.answer: Text Generation, Image Synthesis (image generation), Audio Production, and Video Creation.

params.text:
Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning

All machine learning models are trained using one of two fundamental paradigms, determined by the nature of the training data:

The model learns from data that has been explicitly labelled or categorised by humans prior to training. Input data is paired with the correct output, teaching the model to map inputs to predefined categories. Example: a spam filter trained on emails labelled 'legitimate' or 'spam'.

The model receives raw, unlabelled data and must independently discover inherent patterns, hidden structures, or groupings without any prior categorisation. Example: a customer segmentation model that groups consumers by purchasing behaviour without predefined categories.

panels.title: Why the distinction matters for ethics review

params.text: The choice of learning paradigm has direct ethical implications. Supervised learning requires labelled training data — meaning human annotators made classification decisions that can introduce bias. Unsupervised learning discovers patterns autonomously, but those patterns may reflect and amplify biases present in the raw data. Both require scrutiny.

params.text:
Applied Scenario: Selecting the Right Model

Consider a dataset of communications already explicitly labelled as “legitimate” or “malicious spam”. Because the data carries precise historical labels, supervised machine learning is the correct methodology. Unsupervised learning or an LLM would be inappropriate choices — the structure of the data dictates the training approach.

Effective AI deployment always begins with understanding the structure of the training data before any model design decisions are made.

params.title: Review learning paradigm concepts.

dialogs.answer: A learning paradigm where the model is trained on data that has been explicitly labelled with correct outputs. The model learns to map inputs to predefined categories.
A learning paradigm where the model is trained on unlabelled data and independently discovers patterns, hidden structures, or groupings.

dialogs.text: What type of data does supervised learning require?
dialogs.answer: Labeled data — data that has been explicitly categorised or tagged by humans prior to training.

dialogs.text: What is the primary objective of unsupervised learning?
dialogs.answer: To independently identify inherent patterns, hidden structures, or groupings within a raw dataset without prior categorisation.

dialogs.text: What is the result of training a machine learning algorithm called?
dialogs.answer: The model — the functional component responsible for making predictions and inferences at run-time.

params.text:
What is a Model?

A model is the functional software artifact that results from training a machine learning algorithm on a dataset. It is the component responsible for inference — making predictions on new, unseen data at run-time. Unlike traditional software bugs, finished AI models harbour unique security vulnerabilities tied to their statistical nature.

The Four Attack Types

A broad category of deliberate manipulations during training or inference, designed to compromise an AI model’s accuracy, reliability, or security. A well-known example: adding tiny stickers to a stop sign that causes an autonomous vehicle's AI to misclassify it as a speed limit sign.

Corrupting or manipulating the initial training data before training begins, to inherently bias or break the model from its inception. Example: Amazon's recruitment AI, trained on historical hiring data reflecting past gender discrimination, systematically penalised female candidates — a bias baked in at the data level, not introduced post-deployment.

Techniques used to reverse-engineer a trained model in order to extract sensitive or private data that was used to train it. Example: an attacker queries a healthcare AI model to reconstruct private patient records from its responses, even without direct access to the training database.

Crafting specific inputs at run-time that successfully avoid detection or filtering by the model. Example: a malicious actor crafts spam emails with subtle wording changes that bypass a supervised-learning spam filter.

params.text:
Key Insight for Ethics Review

Because an AI model is structurally shaped by its training environment, its ethical integrity can be compromised through its data supply chain — long before a researcher executes their first prompt. Properly evaluating AI risk requires mapping threats across the system’s entire lifecycle: from data collection, through training, to live deployment.

params.title: Review AI security vulnerabilities.

dialogs.answer: A broad category of deliberate manipulations during training or inference, designed to compromise an AI model’s accuracy, reliability, or security. Example: stickers on a road sign that cause an autonomous vehicle to misidentify it.

Corrupting the initial training data to deliberately bias or break the model before it is ever deployed. Example: Amazon's recruitment tool that penalised female candidates due to biased historical training data.
Techniques used to extract sensitive or private training data directly from a finished, deployed model by querying it in specific ways.
Crafting specific inputs at run-time that successfully bypass a model's detection or filtering mechanisms. Example: spam emails designed to avoid spam filters.

dialogs.text: At what stages can a malicious intervention compromise an AI model?
dialogs.answer: At both stages: during the training phase (data poisoning) and during the inference/run-time phase (adversarial attacks and model evasion).
Amazon's recruitment AI — trained on historically biased hiring data — systematically penalised résumés from female candidates. The bias was embedded in the data, not introduced post-deployment.

params.text:
The Spectrum of AI Capability

The algorithmic capabilities we evaluate today represent a specific point on a much longer evolutionary trajectory. Understanding where current AI sits on this spectrum is essential for calibrated ethical review — neither overstating nor understating the technology’s capabilities.

Systems tightly focused on executing specific, limited tasks. All commercially deployed AI today — spam filters, image classifiers, recommendation algorithms, LLMs — is Narrow AI. These are highly complex, statistics-driven data engines running on physical hardware. They are powerful within their domain; outside it, they fail.

Systems capable of performing a wide range of tasks across multiple domains, rather than being confined to a single function. Current foundation models and large language models show early signs of general-purpose capabilities — they can write, code, summarise, and translate. This intermediate stage is where today's most advanced models sit.

Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is a hypothetical future state characterised by true reasoning, creativity, and consciousness at or beyond human level. AGI would be capable of applying knowledge across any task without retraining. We are not evaluating AGI today — it does not yet exist. Conflating current AI with AGI leads to both over-caution and under-caution in ethical review.

metadata.title: Three Points on the AI Capability Spectrum
metadata.extraTitle: Three Points on the AI Capability Spectrum

params.text:
Practical Implication

When reviewing a research proposal that deploys an AI system, you are evaluating Narrow AI — or, at most, an early form of General-Purpose AI. You are not evaluating a conscious, reasoning entity. A rigorous, demystified understanding of AI’s statistical mechanics and structural vulnerabilities is the non-negotiable prerequisite for proportionate and responsible ethical review.

params.title: Review AI capability concepts.

dialogs.answer: AI systems tightly focused on executing specific, limited tasks. All currently deployed AI is Narrow AI — it is powerful within its domain but cannot generalise beyond it.
AI systems capable of performing a wide range of tasks across various domains. Foundation models and LLMs show early signs of this capability — this is the 'Emerging Reality'.

A hypothetical future AI capable of understanding, learning, and applying knowledge across any task at or beyond human level, with true reasoning, creativity, and consciousness. It does not currently exist.
Reasoning, creativity, and consciousness — applied across any task domain, not limited to a specific function.

dialogs.text: Which current AI technology demonstrates early signs of general-purpose capabilities?
dialogs.answer: Foundation models and Large Language Models (LLMs), which can perform tasks across multiple domains including writing, coding, summarisation, and translation.
Large AI models trained on broad data at scale, which can be adapted to many downstream tasks. They demonstrate early signs of general-purpose capabilities.

Summary: What You Have Learned

Congratulations on completing the Introduction to AI module. Below are the key takeaways from each section.

1. Defining AI & Historical Context

Artificial Intelligence is a field of computer science focused on simulating human intelligence. Its development spans decades — from 1950s foundations through AI winters to the deep learning era that began in the 2010s, driven by big data and computational power.

2. The AI Ecosystem

AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL. Machine Learning is a subfield of AI; Deep Learning is a subset of ML. Not all robots use AI; the term “AI” is often applied as a marketing label for what are technically ML or DL applications. Accurate classification of the technology is prerequisite to proportionate ethical review.

3. Neural Networks

Brain-inspired computing systems with input, hidden, and output layers. The 2012 turning point — when neural networks surpassed traditional ML in accuracy — was enabled by two critical resources: very large datasets and massive computational power. Their primary ethical vulnerabilities are embedded in their training data.

4. NLP & Large Language Models

NLP enables computers to process human language. LLMs generate coherent text through next-word prediction — statistical pattern-matching, not genuine comprehension. The “Illusion of Understanding” must not lead to anthropomorphising LLM outputs in research contexts.

5. Generative AI

Models capable of creating new content — text, images, audio, and video — by extrapolating from training data patterns. All outputs are statistical extrapolations, not original human creativity.

6. Learning Paradigms

Supervised learning requires labelled training data; unsupervised learning discovers patterns in unlabelled data. The structure of the training data determines the appropriate model type — and shapes the ethical risks that must be evaluated.

7. AI Security: Model Vulnerabilities

Finished models are susceptible to four categories of attack: Adversarial Attacks (the broad category of deliberate manipulation during training or inference), Data Poisoning (corrupts training data), Model Inversion (extracts private training data from a deployed model), and Model Evasion (crafted inputs bypass detection at run-time). Ethical risk spans the model’s entire lifecycle.

8. The Spectrum of AI Capability

Current AI = Narrow AI (specific, limited tasks). Emerging: General-Purpose AI (foundation models showing multi-domain capability). Hypothetical future: AGI/Strong AI (human-level reasoning and consciousness across all tasks). We are not evaluating AGI today; calibrated review requires clarity about where current AI sits on this spectrum.

Ready for Sub-Module 2

With this foundational understanding of AI’s architecture, capabilities, and vulnerabilities, you are now equipped to engage with the core frameworks in Sub-Module 2: AI-enabled Research Ethics.

Key Concepts & Further Reading

  • LeCun, Y., Bengio, Y., & Hinton, G. (2015). Deep learning. Nature, 521, 436–444. The foundational paper on deep learning by its pioneers.
  • Russell, S. & Norvig, P. (2020). Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th ed.). Pearson. The standard academic reference on AI fundamentals.
  • European Commission. (2021). Proposal for a Regulation on Artificial Intelligence (AI Act). Brussels: European Commission. The primary EU regulatory framework for AI in research and deployment.
  • Goodfellow, I., Shlens, J., & Szegedy, C. (2014). Explaining and harnessing adversarial examples. arXiv:1412.6572. Foundational paper on adversarial attacks.
